text: When you type into ChatGPT or Claude, it feels like you're talking to something that reads, remembers and thinks. So let's take the chat window away and look underneath. Your app sends some text to the model, and the model sends text back. In training, it read an enormous amount of writing and learned to predict what comes

next. So that's what it does, one small piece at a time, until the answer is finished. The search, the memory, the file uploads: that's all software the app builds around this one call. In this module, that software has a name. It's the harness. Those small pieces are called tokens.

A model doesn't read letters or whole words. It reads chunks of text, and in English a token is about three quarters of a word. Code takes more, and so does another language. And almost everything about an LLM is counted in tokens: what you pay, how fast it answers, and how much you can send.

Every model has a limit on how many tokens it can handle in one call. That's the context window. Your instructions, the conversation so far, any documents you attach, and even the answer it writes back all have to fit inside. Anything outside the window doesn't exist for the model. Bigger windows help, but a full window is

slow and it costs more. So a lot of what you'll build is choosing what goes in. Say a client has five thousand pages of policy. You don't send all of it. You find the five pages that matter for this question, and you send those. That's retrieval. The model also doesn't remember anything between calls. Each call stands alone.

It has no idea what you asked a minute ago, and it doesn't learn from your conversation. When a chatbot remembers your name, that's the app at work: it sends the conversation, or notes about you, again with every message. So each turn of a long chat costs a little more than the last. And resending that history is the first

piece of how an agent works. When the model picks the next token, it isn't certain. It has a list of possible tokens, each with a probability, and it picks one. Temperature controls how adventurous that pick is. Low, and it nearly always takes the most likely token: what you want for pulling fields out of an invoice, or for writing

code. Turn it up when you're brainstorming product names. But even at a low temperature, the same prompt can give two different answers. So you can't judge an AI system by trying it once. That's why we spend so much time on evals: repeatable tests of how often it gets things right. Then there's the bill.

You pay for the tokens you send and the tokens that come back, and output usually costs more. But people forget the input side: you pay for everything you sent, the whole history included, before the model writes a single word. A small model can be many times cheaper than the biggest one. So a common move is to send the easy work to

a small model, and save the big one for the hard cases. Models also come closed or open. Closed models, like Claude or GPT, you reach through the maker's API: nothing to run yourself, but your data leaves your building. Open-weight models, like Llama or Qwen, can run on your own servers. That's why a bank or a hospital often picks

them. In the bootcamp, you'll do both. So here's one API call with everything in place. It names the model. Then the messages: a system message with your instructions, whatever history the app resends, and the user's question. Then the temperature. What comes back is the reply, plus a usage block: how many tokens went in and how many

came out. That's what you pay for. And Claude Code sends a call like this on every turn. Under this video, there are three small demos. Count the tokens in a sentence, watch a model forget, and price a busy day of calls. And think about this: which part of your own chats costs the most?
